title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
This is impersonation, not a model error. Synthetic voice and image tools were used to copy the voices and likenesses of people the victims already trusted, including a South Florida immigration attorney whose identity was used to offer legal services to immigrants. The same techniques were applied to the grandparent scam and to romance and cryptocurrency fraud, where the cloned voice or faked photo is the part that makes an old request credible.

The failure sits outside any system the victims or the impersonated professionals deployed. The generators are consumer tools, and the contact arrives through social media, phone calls and spoofed numbers, so there is no operator, no log and no review step between the fraudster and the target. Catching it required verification through a channel the victim already knew, a call back to a known number or a pre-arranged code word, because nothing in the message itself distinguished the copy from the person.

What is not established is which AI tools were used in any of these cases, or whether each loss counted in the complaint figures involved synthetic media at all. The attorney's account of his identity being used is his account, and the complaint totals are reported complaints rather than adjudicated frauds.

summary:
Scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to commit fraud across Georgia and South Florida by creating deepfakes and cloned voices to impersonate trusted individuals. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans lost nearly $893 million to AI-enabled scams last year, with Florida reporting 350 complaints totaling $39.9 million and Georgia reporting 71 complaints totaling $10.4 million. The technology allows criminals to make old scams more convincing by cloning voices from social media, spoofing phone numbers, creating fake photos, and researching victims' family members to add authenticity to emergency requests.

Authorities warn that AI is making familiar scams harder to recognize, from romance schemes to cryptocurrency fraud to the grandparent scam, where criminals use voice cloning to convince victims their relatives need urgent money. Banks urge customers to verify requests through known phone numbers before acting. State officials recommend families establish code words to confirm identities during emergencies and warn that as AI tools become cheaper and more accessible, the threat will likely worsen. Experts say verification rather than speed is now crucial for protecting oneself from these scams.
